title: Resolving Power of Optical Instruments
short_intro: Resolving power is the capacity of an optical instrument to distinguish between two closely spaced point objects as separate entities. It is fundamentally limited by the wave nature of light causing diffraction.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Rayleigh's criterion of resolution, resolving power of microscopes and astronomical telescopes, dependence on wavelength and aperture size.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of resolving power limits for circular apertures (telescope and microscope), Rayleigh criterion for spectral lines (gratings and prisms), numerical aperture effects.

prerequisites: Fraunhofer diffraction through a single slit and circular aperture

concept_notes.heading: Rayleigh's Criterion for Resolution
bullets: Two equal point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of one falls on the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other.
The angular separation theta between two point objects must be at least equal to the angular radius of the first dark ring of the Airy disc.
If the separation is less than Rayleigh's limit, the combined intensity profile appears as a single broad maximum, rendering the objects unresolved.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of an Astronomical Telescope
bullets: Defined as the reciprocal of the smallest angular separation (dθ) between two distant point objects that can be clearly distinguished.
Given by the expression RP =  rac{1}{d	heta} =  rac{D}{1.22lambda}, where D is the diameter of the objective lens and λ is the wavelength of light.
Increasing the aperture diameter D improves the resolving power and collects more light for faint astronomical objects.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of a Compound Microscope
bullets: Defined as the reciprocal of the minimum linear distance (Δx) between two point objects that can be resolved.

Given by Abbe's criterion: RP =  rac{1}{Delta x} =  rac{2mu sin	heta}{lambda}, where μ is the refractive index of the medium between object and objective, and θ is the semi-vertical angle of the cone of light.
The term μ sin(θ) is known as the numerical aperture (NA) of the microscope objective.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of Diffraction Grating
bullets: Defined as the ability to separate two neighboring spectral lines of wavelengths λ and λ + dλ.
Expressed as RP =  rac{lambda}{dlambda} = n N, where n is the order of the spectrum and N is the total number of rulings on the grating surface.
Higher orders and a greater total number of rulings yield higher spectral resolution.

derivations.title: Resolving Power of a Telescope
derivations.conditions: Fraunhofer diffraction of light from a circular aperture of diameter D
steps: The angular position of the first minimum of a circular aperture diffraction pattern is given by sin	heta approx 	heta =  rac{1.22lambda}{D}.
According to Rayleigh's criterion, two point sources are just resolved if their angular separation equals this minimum angle θ.
Taking the reciprocal, the resolving power of the telescope is defined as RP =  rac{1}{	heta}.

derivations.title: Resolving Power of a Microscope
derivations.conditions: Object placed close to the objective lens in a medium of refractive index μ
steps: The minimum distance for resolution in a medium of refractive index μ considering marginal rays is given by Abbe's theory as Delta x =  rac{lambda}{2mu sin	heta}.
The resolving power is the inverse of this minimum resolvable distance: RP =  rac{1}{Delta x}.
Substituting the expression for Δx yields the final formula.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity Distribution for Two Resolved Point Sources
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two overlapping diffraction intensity curves where the central maximum of one coincides with the first minimum of the other, showing a distinct dip in the resultant middle.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Satisfies Rayleigh criterion; the dip between peaks confirms two distinct sources.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identifies conditions for visual separation in optical instruments.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Unresolved vs. Resolved Diffraction Patterns
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three subplots: (a) Peaks far apart (clearly resolved with deep dip), (b) Rayleigh criterion (dip drops to about 81% of peak), (c) Peaks too close (unresolved single broad maximum).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the transition from resolvable to unresolvable point objects.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual multiple-choice questions on graphical criteria.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Abbe's Microscope Resolution Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a microscope stage with a fine grating illuminated by monochromatic light, showing marginal rays entering the objective lens at angle θ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how higher diffraction orders must enter the objective to resolve finer specimen details (Δx).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining the role of Numerical Aperture in practical microscopy.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the resolving power of a telescope objective of diameter 200 cm for light of wavelength 550 nm.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: D = 200 cm = 2.0 m, λ = 550 nm = 5.5 	imes 10^-7 m.
Use the formula for telescope resolving power: RP =  rac{D}{1.22lambda}.
Substitute values: RP =  rac{2.0}{1.22 	imes 5.5 	imes 10^-7} =  rac{2.0}{6.71 	imes 10^-7}.

solved_numericals.question: A microscope has an objective with a numerical aperture of 0.12. Using light of wavelength 6000 A, find the minimum separation between two points that can be resolved.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: NA = mu sin	heta = 0.12, λ = 6000 A = 6 	imes 10^-7 m.
Use Abbe's criterion for minimum separation: Delta x =  rac{lambda}{2mu sin	heta} (or 0.61λ / NA depending on convention, using standard textbook form Delta x =  rac{lambda}{2 cdot NA}).
Substitute values: Delta x =  rac{6 	imes 10^-7}{2 	imes 0.12} =  rac{6 	imes 10^-7}{0.24}.
Calculate final distance: Delta x = 2.5 	imes 10^-6 m = 2.5 mu m.

solved_numericals.question: Find the minimum number of lines a diffraction grating must have to resolve the sodium doublet lines (λ_1 = 589.0 nm and λ_2 = 589.6 nm) in the second order spectrum.
solution_steps: Use resolving power of grating formula:  rac{lambda}{dlambda} = nN.
Substitute values for order n = 2:  rac{589.3}{0.6} = 2N.
Solve for N: N =  rac{589.3}{1.2} approx 491.

assumptions_and_limitations: Rayleigh's criterion is a subjective limit; two point sources can sometimes be resolved even if they do not strictly meet the intensity dip condition by using image processing or high contrast.
Derivations assume monochromatic, incoherent point sources situated in the object plane.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Magnification and resolving power are the same thing.
common_misconceptions.correct: Magnification only enlarges the image size without adding detail, whereas resolving power determines the ability to reveal fine structural details.
common_misconceptions.why: A blurry image can be magnified infinitely, but it will still lack resolution if diffraction limits are breached.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Decreasing the wavelength of light decreases the resolving power of a microscope.
common_misconceptions.correct: Shorter wavelengths increase the resolving power.
common_misconceptions.why: Since resolving power is inversely proportional to wavelength (λ), reducing λ (e.g., using ultraviolet or electron beams) increases RP.

quick_revision: Telescope resolving power increases with objective diameter D.
Microscope resolving power increases with numerical aperture (μ sin θ) and decreases with wavelength λ.
Grating resolving power depends directly on the product of order and total number of lines (nN).
